conditions.firmware: default configuration built at the base commit and after the change in separate directories under ~/.cache/sunstoneos/build/board-bundles-measure/; cmp of the 13 ELF images; tool is host Python and changes no native source

narrative: Baseline: before the tool existed, a shell ran bwrap --ro-bind / / --dev /dev --proc /proc --tmpfs /sys --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /run --bind DIR DIR --unshare-all --die-with-parent --clearenv ten times with /bin/sh -c : and listed the same views inside and outside the sandbox (host view: 265 entries in /dev, 11 in /sys, 16,918 in /tmp, 69 in /run, 98 environment variables, host network; sandbox start median 4 ms, range 4 to 6 ms, bwrap running sh; earlier note 31 ms for bwrap running sh on this host on 2026-10-22). After: the host check builds AArch64 ELF fixtures with clang-21 and ld.lld, commits fixture preparation modules, two fixture runners and a copy of the supervised transport to a new Git repository, and runs the tool once on 24 fixture rows. A fixture module lists /dev, /sys, /tmp, /run, the network interfaces and the environment from its own process and from a child process, and tries to write outside the run directory. The check reads each row's run.json metrics, stat modes, snapshot manifest and submission, and times the tool's sandbox prefix running /bin/true fifteen times. Results: 14 /dev entries; empty /sys, /tmp and /run; PATH, HOME, LANG and PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE only; loopback interface only; writes outside the run directory fail. Sandbox start median 2.9 to 3.3 ms, maximum 3.5 to 4.1 ms over two runs of the check, bwrap running /bin/true. Bytes read from bundle/ outside prepare() equal the bundle size per prepared row (4,171,290 bytes for the nested fixture of five files); writable entries in bundle/ during the artifact pass 0; one copy of each bundle file (each snapshot holds the row's sources and artifacts.json only); 0 of 3 prepared rows refused by submission(). Monitor images: 0 wrongly accepted of ten injected cases (no symbol table, no monitor_entry, each of the seven prefixes, and a memory image without monitor_renewal_cap). Queue timeout: Monitor 1,200 s; nested fixture 1,118 s, which is its 1,058 s attempt bound recomputed with the transport's transfer_timeout() plus 60 s; without uploads 970 s for the OS-image rows and 930 s for the arbiter row; an existing OS-image bundle of 42 files and 22.9 MB 2,451 s. All six injected row-refusal cases were refused: a Monitor and a Terminal bundle admitted under another schema, a Monitor and a Terminal row without admission values, a runner without COMPLETION_COUNTS, and a 101-file bundle whose bound is 4,061 s (limit 3,600 s). Host check wall time 0.79 s. The fixture run also refused a failing prepare(), an uncommitted source and a missing module on their own rows only, and stopped unknown and excluded input rows before creating a run directory. Firmware: all 13 ELF images byte-identical between the base build and the build after the change, from 162,192 bytes (kernel-check.elf) to 5,065,864 bytes (a733-mimus-usb.elf). Negative control: with --tmpfs /tmp removed from the sandbox prefix, the check fails on the fixture's /tmp listing. Not measured: DDR tested, memory runs per chain, time from entry to forced return, fixed cost per run, re-enumerations per chain and chain wall time; the memory profile and the capped renewal handler did not exist, so no memory bundle could be prepared.

hypothesis: The three-step memory qualification chain tests 12,224 of 12,288 MiB in 4 to 6 monitor runs within 10 minutes of wall time.
prediction: All figures are estimates. Memory qualification estimates 0.9 to 1.6 s per 256 MiB sub-slice. Step 1 marches 960 MiB in 3.4 to 6.0 s and step 2 marches 2,048 MiB in 7.2 to 12.8 s, one run each. Step 3 marches 36 sub-slices in 32 to 58 s, which needs 2 to 4 runs at 18.5 s in the first run (after the 1.5 s signature) and 19 s later; its last run has 1.0 to 15.7 s spare, so the separate final run for the DMA0 cases is needed only near 1.0 or 1.5 s per sub-slice. The chain is 4 to 6 runs, DDR tested 12,224 of 12,288 MiB (baseline 8 KiB, rank 3). Time from entry to forced return: 22 s with capped renewal (baseline 2 s, uncapped by renewal in USB builds). Fixed cost per run (upload, launch, re-enumeration, record read): budget 3 s, estimate 2.0 s because the 2026-10-15 forced-stall run took 4.0 s from its first read to its result file, of which 2 s was the deadline. Two re-enumerations per run, 8 to 12 per chain. Chain wall time budget 10 min: 2.3 to 3.5 min for 4 to 6 runs alone, 8.3 to 9.5 min after ranks 1 to 7. The wall-time replay (wait_needed in tools/usb_guard.py, from the guard state ranks 1 to 7 leave) assumes 22 s per run plus 3 s of fixed cost and at least 60 s from rank 7's last re-enumeration to the first memory run, and counts two re-enumerations each for ranks 4 to 7 and none for ranks 1 to 3, whose code returns to the ROM without resetting its USB stack. Those eight leave room for two memory runs under the guard's cap of 12 per 600 s, so the third waits for the oldest to age out. Memory runs use one Cortex-A55 at the 494 MHz boot clock, so the march is CPU-limited at 1.0 to 1.6 GB/s. Two changes would shorten the chain (estimated): a qualified A55 clock raise to 1.8 GHz would cut march time by about three times and give 3 to 4 runs (needs the user's approval under memory qualification's clock rule and the CPU clock evidence, no secondary-core startup risk); a returning multicore base with eight per-core slices, if DRAM sustains their sum, would give 3 runs but waits for secondary-core startup qualification. Both are left out until approval or qualification exists.
conclusion: Not run: the capped renewal handler and the memory row's admission do not exist, so no memory bundle is prepared. Board records will replace the estimates. Rejected alternative, short runs of 1.6 s without renewal, would need 42 to 100 sessions, 84 to 200 re-enumerations of a board that cannot be reconnected and at least 70 minutes of churn wait, and their 64 MiB sub-slices would weaken memory qualification's bound on cache lines surviving a march element from below e^-32 to about e^-8.
narrative: Step coverage: step 1 960 MiB (0x4400_0000-0x8000_0000, offset bits 6-29), step 2 2,048 MiB (0x8000_0000-0x1_0000_0000, bits 6-31), step 3 9,216 MiB (0x1_0000_0000-0x3_4000_0000, bits 6-33); 64 MiB protected window at 0x4000_0000; DMA0 cases at most 8 transfers of at most 1 MiB, each with a 10 ms deadline; 1.6 s is the 1.5 s signature plus eight 10 ms DMA0 deadlines.

hypothesis: Per-job interrupt, fallback and client wake-up counts show whether interrupt delivery makes the one-tick fallback waits in the GPU and NPU services unnecessary.
prediction: Zero fallback completions over a session would justify removing the tick wait in pvr_gpu_service.c and npu_service.c (performance-architecture section 1.3). The counts are interrupt_completions, fallback_completions and client_wakeups per job, recorded as measurements, not pass conditions.
conclusion: Not run: pvr_gpu_service.c counts no completions; npu_service.c counts irq_completions in irq_progress(), which also runs for transitions the fallback observes, so it does not separate the paths; no runner declares COMPLETION_COUNTS or reports the counts.
narrative: Terminal rows are refused unless the runner declares COMPLETION_COUNTS = ('interrupt_completions', 'fallback_completions', 'client_wakeups').
